header: This is the one place that asks RailRadar (with the plant's key) and keeps the answer. It is shared by the timetable route and the fare route (which looks a train up in the same kept timetable, so that only a real train of Durgapur can cost a fare request). The key (RAILRADAR_API_KEY, in the server's environment) is read here only, put in the Authorization header, never logged, never in an answer and never sent to a browser. The key's quota: I keep the timetable twelve hours twice over, in the host's data cache (next/cache unstable_cache: it outlives restarts and is shared by every copy of the server; a plain fetch cache is switched off by a dynamic route, which is why I do not use it), and in the memory of the route's own copy.

symbols.name: railRadarFetch
doc: One GET to RailRadar with the key; it returns the answer's status and JSON (the callers decide what a status means). It times out after twelve seconds.

symbols.name: loadRailway
doc: Gives the timetable from the host-wide cache (twelve hours); I ask RailRadar only when there is none or it is old.

symbols.name: askBoard
doc: One board of RailRadar, with the statuses that every caller treats in the same way.

symbols.name: askAsansol
doc: Asansol's trains that Durgapur does not stop: I ask two boards (Asansol's, and Durgapur's with the pass-throughs), one after the other, and keep them twelve hours like the Durgapur one (so two requests in twelve hours).

symbols.name: KEPT_ASN_S
doc: I keep Asansol's list THREE days (two requests each time, from the free plan's 100 a month, of which Durgapur's twelve-hour timetable already takes about 60), because the stations a train stops at hardly change from day to day.
